sections.h2: What should a seller know about Gainesville as a place?
sections.html:
Gainesville is the largest city and the county seat of Alachua County, and the city describes itself as the cultural, educational and commercial center of north central Florida. It covers about 65.27 square miles, and the city's 2025 population figure is 151,275, based on University of Florida BEBR data.

The city's own facts page lists a median age of 26.4 and a median household income of $43,783 from 2023 Census data, which reflects a large student population around the University of Florida and Santa Fe College. Gainesville sits on the I-75 corridor, roughly halfway between Atlanta and Miami. The climate listed there is mild winters, warm summers, a January average high of 65 F, a June average high of 89 F, and about 35 inches of rain a year. A seller in a student-heavy area should expect a mix of owner-occupants and investors in the buyer pool.

sections.h2: Who bills a Gainesville property tax bill?
sections.html:
Alachua County bills it. The Alachua County Property Appraiser sets value and exemptions, the Alachua County Tax Collector mails and collects the bill, and the City of Gainesville is one of several taxing bodies whose rates appear on it.

  • Tax collector: phone (352) 374-5236 if no bill arrives in November. Delinquent-tax payment questions go to its Tax Operations Department at (352) 264-6968.
  • Property appraiser: prepares the tax roll and decides homestead, disability, widow and agricultural exemptions. Its tangible division answers at (352) 374-5234.
  • City commission: sets the city millage as part of its annual budget.
  • County commission: sets county millage and certain non-ad valorem assessments.

Non-ad valorem charges on the bill include mandatory refuse collection, rural collection center, solid waste management, paving, water extension, fire, storm water and PACE assessments, according to the tax collector. Lower-income owners may be exempted from some of them through the county social services office at (352) 264-6750.

sections.h2: What is the City of Gainesville millage rate?
sections.html:
The city's facts page lists a millage rate of 6.7297 for fiscal year 2027, which means $6.7297 per $1,000 of taxable value. The city's final millage analysis, labeled as a staff recommendation, shows 6.7297 as the final and current rate, with a rolled-back rate of 6.3839 and a two-thirds vote maximum of 7.0223.

The same analysis says the figures are estimates until the Alachua County Property Appraiser's TRIM notice and the September hearings finalize them, and it gives a certified taxable value of $12,625,373,917 as of July 1, 2026. The city budget page also reports a 6.24 percent rise in taxable property values. A city millage line is only one piece of the total, because the county, school board and water management district bill on the same parcel. Read the final rates on your November bill or ask the tax collector.

sections.h2: When are Alachua County taxes due and what is the discount?
sections.html:
Bills are normally mailed on or before November 1, the full amount is due by March 31, and taxes become delinquent on April 1. The Alachua County Tax Collector lists discounts that step down each month.

Alachua County early-payment discounts as printed by the tax collector
Month paidDiscount
November4%
December3%
January2%
February1%
MarchNone

Source: the Alachua County Tax Collector's property tax page. If a mortgage escrow account pays your tax, the lender requests the bill and you get an information-only copy. The lender must pay during the 4 percent window, and once the loan is paid off the lender has to take your account off its request list, so a seller who has just paid off a mortgage should check the bill is coming to them.

sections.h2: Can I pay Gainesville property tax in installments?
sections.html:
Yes, Alachua County offers a quarterly plan. The prior year's tax must exceed $100, and applications are due by April 30, which for 2026 has passed. The same April 30 date recurs each year.

  • 1st installment, due by June 30, discounted 6 percent.
  • 2nd installment, due by September 30, discounted 4.5 percent.
  • 3rd installment, due by December 31, discounted 3 percent.
  • 4th installment, due by March 31, no discount.

The first two payments are one quarter of the previous year's tax, and the last two split the remaining actual liability. Missing the first payment ends eligibility for that year and a regular November bill follows. If a due date lands on a weekend or holiday it moves to the next working day.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid Gainesville property tax?
sections.html:
On April 1 a 3 percent minimum charge applies to real estate tax, and advertising charges follow in May. The collector advertises each delinquent parcel once a week for three weeks and holds the tax certificate sale online at lienhub.com on or before June 1.

Bidding starts at 18 percent and goes down, and a certificate earns at least 5 percent unless the bid is zero. The certificate is a first lien, valid seven years. The holder can apply for a tax deed when two or more years have passed since delinquency, and the property then goes to public auction. You can pay the collector to remove the lien, and the collector says the payment date in the office decides the exact amount. Delinquent tax can be paid by cash, check, money order, debit card (minimum $2.50 fee), e-check ($1.00) or credit card and PayPal (2.5 percent fee).

sections.h2: How do homestead and the Save Our Homes cap apply in Gainesville?
sections.html:
The city's facts page lists a homestead exemption of up to $50,000. State guidance describes it as $25,000 against all taxes, plus up to $25,000 more on assessed value above $50,000 for non-school taxes. Apply by March 1 with the property appraiser, and the home must be your permanent residence on January 1.

Save Our Homes limits yearly growth in assessed value to the lower of 3 percent or CPI, and a sale resets the next owner to just value on the following January 1. The state cap chart shows 2.7 percent for 2026. The tax collector also offers a homestead deferral, filed by March 31, with interest of no more than 7 percent a year and a limit that the primary mortgage cannot exceed 70 percent of assessed value. All deferred tax and interest come due when ownership changes, so a sale triggers repayment at closing.

sections.h2: What should I do about tax when I sell a Gainesville house?
sections.html:
Order a payoff from the Alachua County Tax Collector, and ask the closing agent to pay it from your proceeds. If you deferred tax, add the deferral balance and interest to the figure. Alachua County Tax Collector pages also say proration of tangible tax on a business or rental is settled between buyer and seller at closing, so ask the agent how any personal property tax is treated.

The deed carries Florida documentary stamp tax at 70 cents per $100 of consideration, paid to the clerk when the deed is recorded, and the Revenue Department says all parties are liable no matter who agrees to pay it. Rental owners should confirm no tangible personal property bill is open, since that lien survives a sale. A cash buyer can often close in days, which suits a seller facing the April 1 delinquency or a certificate sale.

faqs.q: What is the Gainesville millage rate?
faqs.a: The city's facts page lists 6.7297 for fiscal year 2027, but the city's final analysis calls it a staff recommendation. Check the final rate on your bill or with the Alachua County Tax Collector.
The Alachua County Tax Collector. If you do not get a November bill, call (352) 374-5236.

faqs.q: When is Alachua County property tax late?
faqs.a: After March 31. Taxes become delinquent April 1, and a 3 percent minimum charge is added.

faqs.q: Is the Gainesville installment plan still open?
faqs.a: The 2026 application deadline of April 30 has passed. The plan recurs each year with an April 30 application deadline, and the first payment is due by June 30.

faqs.q: Does a sale end my homestead deferral?
faqs.a: The deferral becomes due, with interest, when ownership changes. The closing agent should pay the balance from your proceeds.
